hints: Notice the statement is about currents entering a junction compared with currents leaving the same junction.
Recall that current is rate of flow of charge, $I = \Delta Q / \Delta t$, so the currents measure charge per second.
Ask what would happen to charge at the junction if entering charge per second did not equal leaving charge per second.
walkthrough: Identify the rule given: at any junction, sum of currents in equals sum of currents out. This is Kirchhoff's first law.
Recall the definition of current as rate of flow of charge: $I = \Delta Q / \Delta t$.
Apply charge conservation: charge cannot be created, destroyed or stored at a steady junction, so the amount of charge $\Delta Q$ arriving in time $\Delta t$ must equal the amount leaving.
Dividing that charge balance by time gives balance of currents: $\Sigma I_{in} = \Sigma I_{out}$.
Energy and e.m.f. ideas relate to work done per charge around a loop, not to counting charge at a junction. This is option A.

options.A: Charge cannot be created or destroyed at a junction, so total charge arriving per second must equal total charge leaving per second.
options.B: Electromotive force is energy per unit charge from the source and is not conserved at a junction in this way.
options.C: Conservation of energy leads to the loop rule about e.m.f. and potential drops, not the junction rule about currents.
options.D: Potential difference is shared around loops, but the junction statement compares currents, not voltages.
